events.c: The pilot and navigator left Lae aboard the aircraft.
A forecast of stronger winds and rain arrived during takeoff. Whether the crew received it is unknown.
The first clear radio report to Lae put the aircraft at 7,000 feet.
The aircraft reported flying at 10,000 feet. Thick clouds prompted a planned descent.
The last report heard at Lae placed the aircraft above clouds. Its position and altitude remain uncertain.
Nauru heard a report of a ship sighting, but it did not establish the aircraft’s position.
Itasca heard a voice through static, attributed to the aircraft. It provided no useful position.
The pilot said she would listen for radio messages every half hour.
A broken radio message mentioned partly cloudy weather; the full weather description is uncertain.
The pilot requested a radio direction measurement and estimated the aircraft was about 200 miles away.
The crew again requested a radio direction measurement, estimating about 100 miles away without giving a direction.
Itasca could not reliably measure the aircraft’s direction on that radio frequency and requested another. No answer followed.
The pilot reported low fuel. The exact amount remaining is unknown.
The pilot reported flying at 1,000 feet without seeing the ship. The aircraft’s position remained unknown.
The pilot reported circling and requested a radio signal. Itasca transmitted one.
The crew heard Itasca’s signals but could not use them to determine the ship’s direction.
The pilot’s final call described a navigation line but gave no reference point.
Itasca listened on another radio frequency, but no further understandable aircraft reply was heard.
Whether another north or south message followed is uncertain; the exact timing is disputed.
Itasca began searching northward, although the aircraft’s route was unknown.
Unverified distress signals redirected searches around Howland and toward the Phoenix Islands.
Three aircraft searched Gardner and saw signs of recent habitation, but found no aircraft or response.
The Navy search ended without finding the aircraft or crew. Searchers believed they were lost at sea.
A photograph showed an object near Gardner’s reef. Its identification as aircraft landing gear remains disputed.
An anonymous bottle message alleged captivity in the Marshalls. Its author and the crew’s identity remained unverified.
A partial skeleton and nearby objects were found on Gardner. The person’s identity and exact location remained uncertain.
An examiner assessed the remains as male. The bones have not been located for modern testing.
Japan’s investigation found no basis for claims of execution on Saipan, but did not locate the aircraft.
Anthropologists supported the original male assessment, but the missing bones prevented a firm conclusion.
A photograph offered as captivity evidence appeared in a 1935 book, before the crew disappeared.
A study found bone measurements similar to the pilot’s estimated proportions, but did not identify the remains.
A navigation instrument number linked to USS Bushnell weakened the claim that its box belonged to the navigator.
An expedition found no aircraft parts near Nikumaroro. Some areas and the possibility of survivors there remained unresolved.
A sonar image suggested a possible aircraft, but its shape did not confirm its identity.
The sonar target proved to be a natural rock formation.
An expedition was proposed to inspect a possible aircraft in a lagoon. Permit and seasonal delays postponed it.
Newly released historical records became available, without establishing a new crash site.
Inspection found the suspected aircraft was likely coated tree debris. Other recovered objects were not confirmed aircraft parts.

one_line: The pilot and navigator disappeared after failing to locate Howland Island on their flight from Lae.
status_why: Radio contacts document the failed approach, but the crew’s final location and what happened afterward remain unknown.
